title: RBI Eases EDF Filing for Service Exporters With Rs 10 Lakh Route
excerpt: Under the FEMA regulations in force since October 1, service exporters file one monthly EDF, small bills close on self-declaration, and individuals doing personal-nature work were told they do not have to report.
body:
• India's service exporters now declare exports on a single Export Declaration Form (EDF) under the FEMA (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, in force since October 1, 2026.
  • For any single invoice up to Rs 10 lakh, a bank can close the export-monitoring entry on the exporter's own declaration that payment was realised — the threshold is per bill, not per year, and declarations can be filed quarterly in bulk.
  • Business exporters file one EDF per month, within 30 days of the end of the month in which the invoice was raised, through their authorised dealer bank.
  • RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra clarified on October 7 that individuals doing personal-nature work — overseas tutoring and small software assignments were his examples — do not have to report, irrespective of the amount; the RBI's detailed FAQs are still awaited.

Freelancers, consultants and software firms in India who bill overseas clients are working under a new reporting rulebook. The Reserve Bank of India's Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 — Notification No. FEMA 23(R)/2026-RB, amended up to September 22, 2026 — took effect on October 1, 2026 and replaced the 2015 export regulations. The centrepiece is a single Export Declaration Form, or EDF, for exports of goods, services and software.

Who is affected

The regulations cover exporters of services — a category that includes software companies, SaaS startups, agencies and firms billing foreign clients — who must declare the full export value of their services. Software exporters previously filed SOFTEX forms while goods followed a separate declaration process; the new framework unifies them under the EDF, according to Inc42. The group caught off guard was individual freelancers and creators, who feared every overseas payment would need institutional-style paperwork. The RBI addressed that group directly, below.

What changed, precisely

Under Regulation 3(2) of the notification, an exporter of services must furnish an EDF to the specified authority within 30 days from the end of the month in which the invoice was raised. One EDF can cover all of a month's service exports to one or more recipients. For services, the specified authority is the exporter's authorised dealer (AD) bank; software exporters can file with the AD bank or the Software Technology Parks of India. Banks and authorised dealers handle the reporting to the RBI, Inc42 reported.

The Rs 10 lakh relief works like this: where an invoice is up to Rs 10 lakh, or its foreign-currency equivalent, the entry in the Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS) may be closed on the exporter's own declaration that the payment has been realised in full or otherwise, the RBI notification states. That declaration can instead be submitted quarterly for bulk closure of entries. The threshold applies per bill, not to annual export earnings, Inc42 reported — annual earnings above Rs 10 lakh do not by themselves rule out the simplified route for an eligible bill. A reduced realisation on a bill up to Rs 10 lakh can also be permitted on the exporter's declaration, under Regulation 6.

"Banks and authorised dealers would handle reporting to the RBI, while exporters could use self-declaration for bills of up to Rs 10 lakh."

— Inc42, summarising Governor Sanjay Malhotra's clarification

The relief for resident individuals

At the October monetary policy press conference, Governor Sanjay Malhotra clarified that individuals undertaking transactions of a personal nature would not have to report them, and cited earnings from overseas tutoring and small software assignments among the transactions that would not require reporting, Inc42 reported. Deputy Governor Rohit Jain said the framework aims to simplify trade processes and give authorised dealers greater flexibility, and that the RBI would issue FAQs to clarify the requirements. Those FAQs had not been issued in the reporting Inc42 published, so individuals working in their own name should confirm how their AD bank is applying the clarification until the written guidance appears.

Deadlines that still apply

For covered exporters, export proceeds must generally be realised and repatriated within nine months of the invoice date for services, the notification states. Where the export is invoiced or settled in Indian rupees, the period is twelve months, and an authorised dealer may extend the period on request if satisfied with the reasons given. If proceeds remain unrealised beyond one year after the due date or any extension, further exports require full advance payment or an irrevocable letter of credit, Inc42 reported.

What to do next

If you export services through a company, LLP or firm, the action is procedural: file the monthly EDF through your AD bank within 30 days of month-end, keep invoices aligned with receipts, and use the self-declaration route for bills up to Rs 10 lakh. If you work as an individual in your own name, the Governor's clarification says personal-nature work does not require reporting — but with the FAQs still awaited, a short confirmation with your bank is the prudent step before you rely on it.
nri_angle: Indian freelancers and firms billing overseas clients — including clients in the US — now declare service exports under one monthly EDF, with a per-bill Rs 10 lakh self-declaration route.
author: Diaspora Desk
